title: Lesson 1 Quiz: Income, Spending, and Budgeting
description: A short quiz to check what you learned in this lesson. Submitting it completes the lesson's quiz requirement, and your score is recorded separately.

history.note: AI-written question draft. Not reviewed or approved by a human (admin); do not give to students.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: Maya's weekly pay stub shows gross pay of $640. Deductions are $88 for taxes and $32 for a retirement plan contribution. What is her net (take-home) pay for the week, in dollars? (Enter a number only.)
Which of these is the best example of a variable expense for a student?

choices.text: A phone plan that costs $40 each month
Snacks and eating out, which change from month to month
A monthly bus pass sold at a set price
A streaming subscription billed at a flat monthly fee

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: Two students each pay $60 a month for a car insurance policy. Student A drives to a night job with no bus service. Student B lives next to a train station and drives mainly on weekends for fun. How should each classify the expense?

choices.text: Both should call it a want, because insurance is optional spending
Both should call it a variable need, because prices can change
Both should call it a need, because the bill arrives each month
It is a fixed need for A and closer to a fixed want for B

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: Leo wants $1,100 for a used scooter in 6 months. He has already saved $260. Ignoring interest, how much must he save each month to reach the goal on time, in dollars? (Enter a number only.)

Hypothetical example: Rosa's net income is $1,800 a month, but her planned spending and saving add up to $1,950. She notices her gross pay is $2,150. Which response is the best way to make her budget consistent with the budget identity?

choices.text: Cut variable wants (or raise net income) so spending plus saving equals net income
Base the budget on $2,150 gross pay, since that covers the $1,950 plan
Keep the plan and cover the $150 gap each month with a credit card
Stop saving until spending fits, since saving matters less than spending
